Description: A 9th-century BC stele of Kilamuwa, king of Sam'al (reigned about 840-810 BC, son of Haya), found in 1902 at the entrance to Building J during the German Oriental Society excavations at Zincirli Höyük (Sam'al), led by Felix von Luschan and Robert Koldewey. Its 16 lines, in Phoenician language written in an Old Aramaic form of the Phoenician alphabet, record Kilamuwa dismissing his predecessors ('he did nothing') and calling on the king of Assyria for help against powerful neighbors after the Danunians overmastered him. It is now in the Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin.
Interpretations: The stele shows the diplomacy of small Iron Age kings caught between powerful neighbors and Assyria, the same pattern as Ahaz's appeal to Tiglath-Pileser in 2 Kings 16, offered here as a background parallel only, not as a shared event. The relief shows Kilamuwa holding a wilted lotus, a symbol of a dead king, addressing deities.
BiblicalSignificance: It illustrates how small Levantine kings survived by appealing to Assyria, the same diplomatic pattern seen when Ahaz of Judah appealed to Tiglath-Pileser.
